1030.title: The teachers, closed
1030.hook: from Nagarjuna to the village grandmother
1030.howItsDone: Buddhists honor their teachers in chants of lineage, in portraits on altars and in memorial days, while the texts point to the teaching itself as the teacher after the Buddha.

segments.voice: Yesterday: carika, Assaji on his alms round, and Sariputta following because of how he moved. Your line: by example.

Lay them out like photographs on a long table. Nagarjuna, arguing that nothing stands on its own. Asanga, bending over a wounded dog. Shantideva, the monk the others thought was lazy, standing up to recite. Atisha keeping his bad-tempered cook. Milarepa hauling stones for towers he was told to tear down. Machig Labdron offering her body to fear. Dogen just sitting. Hakuin saying is that so. Ryokan wishing he could give a thief the moon. The nun Chiyono and her broken bucket. Ajahn Chah in the forest, Dipa Ma in her small apartment, Maha Ghosananda walking for peace. And at the end, a photo with no name. A grandmother.

Here's what's strange: the Buddha seemed to see this long run of teachers coming, and to warn against leaning on any one of them too hard. In the discourse on his final passing, Ananda is worried about what happens when the Buddha is gone. The answer, in T. W. Rhys Davids' translation: "be ye lamps unto yourselves. Be ye a refuge to yourselves." Just before that, he tells Ananda he has no closed fist of a teacher, nothing kept back for a chosen few. And near the end, as this path heard a few days ago, he says the teaching and the discipline will be their teacher after he is gone. So in the Buddha's own words, the real teacher is the teaching. Every name on that table carried it for a stretch and handed it on. Nagarjuna's logic and the grandmother's lamp-lighting aren't competing; they're two people holding the same lamp at different points on the road. Some were brilliant, some wild, some quiet. Some were saints in their tradition's eyes, and this block also made room for teachers who failed. None of them is the point. The lamp is the point. The Pali word for a teacher is acariya, and in this light a good acariya points past themselves, toward the teaching. Whoever practices today is somewhere on that table, holding the lamp for a while.

Choose one face from the table, a famous name, your grandmother, the stranger who once told you the truth, and pick just one moment: a dog, a bucket, a cup of tea, a word. Let that moment sit beside you while you breathe. If your mind wanders off, come back to it, the way you'd come back to a friend's voice in a noisy room.
The teachers. From Nagarjuna to the grandmother with no name, people who carried the teaching for a stretch, while, in the Buddha's words, the teaching itself stayed the teacher.
Your line: they carried it. None of them was the point; the lamp was. That's day one thousand thirty.

1031.title: Why tell hard history
1031.hook: the tradition is made of people, and people fail and endure
1031.howItsDone: Buddhist monastics recite the Vinaya, which records the incidents behind its rules, including quarrels and misconduct, and Buddhist teachers and historians also discuss the community's failures openly alongside its achievements.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the teachers, closed, from Nagarjuna to the grandmother with no name. Your line: they carried it.

In the town of Kosambi, the monks are fighting. It started small, over whether one monk had broken a rule or not. Now the community has split in two. They argue in the meeting hall. They argue in the village. The Buddha himself comes and asks them to stop, and, the texts say, they tell him, more or less, to leave it to them. This is the Buddha's own community, in his own lifetime, kept and recited by the very tradition it embarrasses. Today opens a new stretch of the path: history held honestly. Why tell the hard parts at all?

The quarrel at Kosambi is told in the Vinaya and in the Majjhima Nikaya, and it doesn't end with a miracle. The Buddha tries to reconcile them. Then he leaves, walking alone into the forest, and the texts describe him visiting a few monks living together in harmony, as if to see what a good community looks like. Then something ordinary happens back in Kosambi. The lay followers, the people who feed the monks, decide that monks who won't make peace get neither their respect nor their alms. Hungry and embarrassed, the monks go and make it up. The Dhammapada has a verse that tradition links to this quarrel. In Max Muller's translation: "The world does not know that we must all come to an end here;—but those who know it, their quarrels cease at once." So here's one answer to today's question. The tradition tells hard history because its own texts do. The sangha, the community, is made of people. People argue, get proud, misuse power, and also repair, apologize and endure. A story where the community never fails would be hard to believe, and harder to learn from. Over the next days: kings who protected monks and kings who used them, persecutions, monks who spoke for war and monks who marched for peace. None of it is told to score a point against Buddhists, and none of it is the whole picture. It's told the way Kosambi is told: plainly, with the failure and the repair side by side.

Bring to mind a hard story from a group you belong to, a family, a team, a school, a faith, not the worst one, a medium one, and let it be true without arguing or defending anyone. Notice where it lands in the body, the jaw, the chest, the stomach, and breathe into that place. Then, if you can, find one person in that story who tried to repair something, and hold both.
Sangha. The community, made of people who fail and repair, and the texts themselves tell it, as at Kosambi.
Your line: made of people. Even the Buddha's own monks quarreled, and made it up. See you tomorrow.

1032.title: Kings and monks
1032.hook: rulers have protected the sangha and used it; both are true
1032.howItsDone: In some Buddhist countries today, governments still recognize, fund or regulate the sangha, and Buddhists debate how close monks should stand to political power.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the sangha, the quarreling monks of Kosambi, brought round by their own lay followers. Your line: made of people.

A king wants a war. King Ajatasattu of Magadha has decided to attack his neighbors, the Vajjians, and first he sends his chief minister to the Buddha. Tell him I'm going to attack, the king says, then come back and report exactly what he says. A strange errand: a ruler using a holy man as a source of intelligence. The Buddha doesn't answer the minister directly. He turns to Ananda, who is fanning him, and asks how the Vajjians live. That's how the discourse on the Buddha's final passing opens: with a king, a war plan, and a teacher who won't simply be used.

The Buddha's questions are about the Vajjians' habits. Do they meet often, and in harmony? Do they honor their elders? Do they protect their shrines and the holy people living among them? As long as they do, he says, they can be expected to prosper, not decline. The minister draws his own conclusion and leaves. Then the Buddha gives his monks a matching list for the sangha. The point is quiet but sharp: a community's strength is in how it lives, not in who is fighting on its side. That's a good lens for the long history of kings and monks, because rulers have done both to the sangha: protected it, and used it. The emperor Ashoka is one well-known case. His own inscriptions, carved in stone, express remorse over his conquest of Kalinga and speak of a new aim, conquest by dhamma. He supported monks and sent out envoys. Tradition, especially in Sri Lanka's chronicles, also says royal power was used to expel monks the court judged false. Protection and control arrived in the same hand. Across Asia, the pattern repeats in different forms. Kings built monasteries and appointed heads of the order. They also leaned on the robe to make their rule look blessed. The Pali texts have a word for the ideal: dhammaraja, a king who rules by dhamma. History holds rulers who reached for that ideal and rulers who borrowed the title. Both are true, and the tradition's own texts keep the question open.

Think back over the last day or two and find one moment when someone used power: a boss, a parent, a government, a platform, you. Ask the Buddha's kind of question: did it protect someone, did it use someone, could it have done both? Stay with the picture, breathing, until you can see both sides without rushing to a verdict.
Dhammaraja. The ideal king who rules by dhamma. Rulers have protected the sangha and used it, sometimes in the same breath, from Ajatasattu's errand to Ashoka's edicts and beyond.
Your line: protected and used. A community's strength is in how it lives. Day one thousand thirty-two.

1033.title: Persecutions
1033.hook: monasteries closed in Tang China and temples torn down in Japan when Buddhism was split from the state
1033.howItsDone: Buddhist communities in China and Japan remember these persecutions in their histories, and temples that were closed or destroyed have in places been rebuilt and are active today.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the dhammaraja ideal, Ajatasattu's errand, Ashoka's remorse, the sangha held close by power. Your line: protected and used.

A bronze Buddha goes into a furnace and comes out as coins. That scene, or one like it, belongs to a stretch of Chinese history when an emperor of the Tang dynasty turned on the monasteries. A Japanese monk named Ennin happened to be traveling in China then, and he kept a diary: monks and nuns sent back to lay life, temples emptied, images taken away, foreign monks like himself ordered to leave. Yesterday the power that protected the sangha also used it. Today it turns against it.

Start with China. Under the Tang emperor Wuzong, the court ordered monasteries closed and their lands and metal taken, and monks and nuns were made to return to ordinary life. Accounts point to more than one reason: money, land, bronze, and court politics that favored other teachings. Ennin's diary is one of the eyewitness sources. Now Japan, much later. A new government set out to separate Buddhist and Shinto institutions, which had been woven together for a long time, and in some regions a movement rose under a harsh slogan, haibutsu kishaku: abolish the Buddha, destroy Shakyamuni. Temples were closed or torn down, images burned or sold, and some monks forced out of their robes. Neither story is told to cast anyone as a villain. Each is told because it happened. Then the second half, today's line: it endured. In China, practice went on, in small temples, in homes, in the chanting of the Buddha's name, and later rulers allowed monasteries again. In Japan, temples were rebuilt and communities regathered. The Buddha's last words, in the discourse on his final passing, already pointed at this. In Rhys Davids' translation: "Decay is inherent in all component things! Work out your salvation with diligence!" Buildings are component things. So is bronze. So are estates. What came through the furnace was people, still practicing.

Bring to mind something in your life, or your family's, that came through a hard time: a recipe carried across a border, a prayer a grandparent kept saying when it wasn't safe, a friendship that survived a bad year. Notice that the building, the job, the house may be gone, and the thing itself is still here. Breathe with it, and let yourself honor it.
Persecutions. Times when rulers turned on monasteries, in Tang China and in Japan, and took the buildings, but not the practice.
Your line: it endured. The furnace took the bronze, not the people. Day one thousand thirty-three, done.

1034.title: Zen and war
1034.hook: some Japanese Buddhist institutions supported the war effort, and some later apologized
1034.howItsDone: Some Japanese Buddhist schools have issued formal statements of repentance for their wartime support, and Buddhist teachers today often point to the first precept and to this history when they speak about violence.

segments.voice: Yesterday: persecutions, monasteries closed in Tang China, temples torn down in Japan, and practice going on in homes. Your line: it endured.

A professional soldier, the head of a band of warriors, comes to the Buddha with a question. His teachers have told him that a warrior who dies fighting bravely goes to a heaven. What does the Buddha say? Don't ask me that, the Buddha says. The soldier asks again. Finally the Buddha answers, and it isn't what the soldier hoped. A mind set on killing in that moment, he says, leads to a bad rebirth, not a heavenly one. He weeps, not because he's insulted, he says, but because he was deceived for so long. Today's story is about Buddhists who set that scene aside.

The first of the precepts that lay Buddhists take is to abstain from taking life. The Dhammapada puts the reason simply. In Max Muller's translation: "All men tremble at punishment, all men fear death; remember that you are like unto them, and do not kill, nor cause slaughter." Now the hard history. In the years leading up to and during the Second World War, some Japanese Buddhist institutions and teachers supported the war effort. Some Zen teachers wrote that the calm of Zen training and the soldier's readiness to die were the same thing, and that killing in the emperor's war could be selfless. Temples raised support for the war, and sermons blessed it. Not every Buddhist in Japan; some resisted and paid for it. But it was real, public, and in the language of practice. After the war, the reckoning came slowly. Then some Japanese Buddhist organizations, including Zen schools and Pure Land schools, issued formal statements of apology. They named their wartime support as wrong, and some said it betrayed the Buddha's teaching. Why tell this in a lesson about practice? Because the soldier's question never goes away. Again and again, someone will say that violence for the right side is holy, and that a calm mind can do it cleanly. The Buddha's answer to the soldier, and the first precept, sit in the texts as a check. And the apologies show a tradition reading its own scriptures again and saying, publicly, we got this wrong.

Recall one thing you once defended, said or went along with that you now see differently; something small is enough. Don't argue your case or pile on blame; just let it be true, like a heavy coat on your shoulders, breathing in knowing it, breathing out staying. If a wish to make it right comes up, let that be there too.
Panatipata veramani. The first precept, to abstain from taking life, broken when some Japanese Buddhist institutions blessed a war, and later apologized publicly.
Your line: apologies made. The first precept was in the texts the whole time. That's day one thousand thirty-four.

1035.title: Sri Lanka's war
1035.hook: in the long civil war, monks spoke both for war and for peace
1035.howItsDone: In Sri Lanka and elsewhere, Buddhist monks and lay groups hold peace walks, interfaith services and loving-kindness meditations for victims of violence on all sides, and Buddhists continue to debate the role of monks in politics.

segments.voice: Yesterday: panatipata veramani, the first precept, set aside to bless a war, and the apologies that came later. Your line: apologies made.

Two clans stand on either side of a river, weapons out. The river is the Rohini, the water is low, and each side says it needs the water for its fields. They are the Buddha's own relatives, on his father's side and his mother's. Tradition says the Buddha walks out between the two lines and asks a simple question: which is worth more, the water or the blood of these men? The only answer is to put the weapons down, and the story says they did. The robe, standing between armies. Today the robe stands on both sides of a real war.

Sri Lanka lived through a long civil war between the government and an armed separatist group, the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam. Civilians suffered on every side: Sinhalese, Tamil, Muslim, Buddhist, Hindu, Christian. Monks were part of it in more than one way. Some spoke against peace talks and for a military victory, and some went into politics and campaigned on it. Some pointed to the island's old chronicle, the Mahavamsa. In one passage, after a war, a remorseful king is told by monks that the people he killed hardly counted, because they didn't follow the Buddha. Scholars and Buddhists argue about that passage, and many say it sits uneasily beside the first precept. Other monks walked a different road. They joined peace marches and interfaith gatherings, sat with families on the other side, and spoke against revenge after attacks. Lay Buddhist movements held peace meditations, people sitting together to wish for an end to the killing. And the Dhammapada has verses that tradition ties to the river quarrel itself. In Max Muller's translation: "Let us live happily then, not hating those who hate us! among men who hate us let us dwell free from hatred!" Which monks were the real Buddhists? This path won't rank them; it tells what each side said and which texts they reached for. The river story is in the tradition. So is the chronicle. Today's line names the monks who reached for the river: monks for peace.
screen: `SOME MONKS FOR WAR, CITING A CHRONICLE.`

If you pray, pray for peace there in words from your own tradition; if you don't, use the old wish from the discourse on loving-kindness: may all beings be happy, may they be safe. Let it include everyone there, both sides, the soldiers and the grandmothers, then let it reach someone you yourself are in a small war with.
Metta. Loving-kindness, the heart of the peace meditations held during Sri Lanka's long civil war.
Your line: monks for peace. Water or blood: the question still stands. See you tomorrow.

1036.title: Myanmar
1036.hook: monks marched for their people; some monks have also spread hatred, and others have opposed them
1036.howItsDone: In Myanmar, giving food and gifts to monks is part of daily life for Buddhists, and the overturned bowl is a formal Vinaya act; monks and lay Buddhists there and abroad remain divided on nationalism, and some lead interfaith work for peace.

segments.voice: Yesterday: metta in Sri Lanka's war, and monks on both sides of it. Your line: monks for peace.

Rows of monks in deep red robes walk through the streets of Yangon in the rain. They aren't shouting. Some are chanting the discourse on loving-kindness. And some carry their alms bowls upside down. On the news it looks like a protest sign. To people who know the monastic rules, it's older and precise: we will not accept your offerings. The monks were refusing gifts from the generals who ruled the country, at a time of hardship for ordinary people. Where giving to monks is part of daily life, that refusal said a great deal without words.

The upturned bowl comes from the Vinaya. In the Cullavagga, a layman falsely accuses a respected monk, and the Buddha allows the sangha to turn the bowl down toward him: the monks won't visit his house or accept his food until he makes amends. It's a formal act, meant to be reversed when the person changes. So when monks in Myanmar turned their bowls down to the generals, they were using an ancient rule as a nonviolent strike. The marches were met with force; monks were beaten and arrested, and monasteries were raided. That's one face of the robe in modern Myanmar. Here's another, and it's hard. In the years since, some monks have preached against Muslims, including the Rohingya, spreading fear and hatred in sermons and online, while violence against Rohingya communities drove families from their homes. Those monks wore the same robe. And a third face. Other monks have spoken out against that hatred, sheltered Muslim neighbors during riots, and joined interfaith efforts, sometimes at real risk. The Dhammapada says, in Max Muller's translation: "Let a man overcome anger by love, let him overcome evil by good." This week ran from the last of the teachers into hard history: the lamp carried, a community made of people, kings, persecutions, a war blessed then apologized for, monks for war and for peace. And now the same robe, used to refuse tyranny, to spread hatred, to shelter neighbors. Today's line holds on to the faces that refuse and shelter: the robe for peace.

Remember the last time you heard someone speak with contempt about a group of people, a joke, a post, a comment at dinner, maybe your own, and without punishing yourself or them, notice what it does in the body. Then picture answering it calmly with one sentence, the way a monk turns a bowl over: no shouting, just a clear refusal. Rehearse that sentence in your mind.
Myanmar. Where monks turned their bowls over to refuse the generals, where some spread hatred, and others stood against it.
Your line: the robe for peace. An upturned bowl can refuse without a single shout. Day one thousand thirty-six.

fork.setup: you're a monk. the rulers are hurting your people, and the only gift you have to give or withhold is your bowl. what do you do?
options: accept their offerings as usual.
turn your bowl over and refuse their gifts.
pick up a weapon.
fork.reveal: monks turned their bowls over, using an ancient Vinaya act as a nonviolent refusal of the generals' offerings.

original.note: Pali patta: the alms bowl; overturning it (patta-nikkujjana) is a formal act of refusal.

chat.says: Why did monks in Myanmar carry their alms bowls upside down?
options: It's an old Vinaya act: refusing offerings, here the generals', until amends are made.
It was a sign of mourning; monks flip their bowls whenever a leader dies.
It meant the monks were giving up their robes and leaving for good.
chat.meaning: In the Vinaya, the sangha can turn the bowl down toward someone and refuse their food until they make amends. The monks used it to refuse the generals.

Yangon.meaning: a city in Myanmar where the monks marched

Rohingya.meaning: a largely Muslim people of Myanmar
